Shoe
shoo
n. (a covering for the foot; rendering Hebrew na'al, Greek hypodema, sandalion)
Old English sceoh. In Scripture the shoe is rarely just footwear: it marks holy ground when removed, transfers a legal right when handed over, and measures a man's rank by who is fit to carry or untie it.

Biblical Definition

The shoe in Scripture is a legal and ceremonial object. Removing it acknowledges holiness: “put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5) — the ground was not holy the day before, and Moses is barefoot because God is there. Handing it over transfers a right: “this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing, for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel” (Ruth 4:7), which is how the nearer kinsman formally surrenders his claim and Boaz becomes the redeemer of Naomi's field and of Ruth. Deuteronomy gives the shaming version of the same rite, where the widow of a man who refuses to raise up his brother's name looses his shoe and spits in his face (Deuteronomy 25:9). And carrying or unloosing another man's shoes is the work of the lowest servant, which is why John the Baptist chooses it to measure the distance between himself and the One coming: “whose shoes I am not worthy to bear” (Matthew 3:11), and in Mark, not worthy to stoop down and unloose. Paul then puts shoes on the Christian: “your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6:15) — a soldier's footwear, for standing firm and for going.

Webster 1828 Definition

Rarely mere footwear. Shoes come off on holy ground; a shoe handed over transfers a legal right, as when Boaz becomes redeemer; carrying another's shoes is the lowest servant's work, which John invokes; and Paul shoes the Christian with the gospel of peace.

expand to see more

SHOE, n. plu. shoes. [Sax. sceo.] A covering for the foot, usually of leather, composed of a thick species for the sole, and a thinner kind for the vamp and quarters.

2. A plate of iron nailed to the hoof of a horse.

3. Among the Hebrews, the delivery of a shoe was a token of the transfer of a right or possession. Ruth 4.

4. To put off the shoes was a mark of reverence, as before holy ground. Ex. 3.

5. To bear or unloose the shoes of another was the office of the meanest slave.

Key Scripture

Exodus 3:5 — "And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground."

Ruth 4:7 — "Now this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing, for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel."

Matthew 3:11 — "I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:"

Ephesians 6:15 — "And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;"

Modern Corruption

The Ruth shoe-ceremony is read as quaint local colour rather than as the legal machinery of redemption — and Exodus 3:5 is generalised into a sacred-places piety that Scripture's own trajectory dismantles.

expand to see more

Ruth 4 is often preached as a love story with an odd procedural interruption, but the shoe is the hinge of the book. Israel's law of redemption required a kinsman with the right, the means, and the willingness; the nearer kinsman had the first two and lacked the third, because redeeming Ruth would mar his own inheritance. He publicly surrenders his claim by handing over his shoe, and Boaz redeems field and widow together before ten elders. Every element is a type discharged in Christ — the kinsman who alone has the right, who pays the whole price, who takes a bride out of a foreign nation, and who does it at cost to himself where another would not. Luke traces the genealogy through this transaction. Treating the shoe as folklore removes the legal architecture that makes redemption a category rather than a sentiment.

Exodus 3:5 has been generalised in the other direction into a theology of sacred space: certain buildings, grounds, and objects are holy in themselves, and reverence consists in ritual behaviour toward them. The verse says the opposite of what is drawn from it. The ground is holy because God is there — it is a bush in a desert, not a shrine, and it is not recorded as venerated afterwards. Scripture's trajectory moves steadily away from holy places: the Lord Jesus tells the woman at the well that the hour comes when neither in this mountain nor at Jerusalem will men worship the Father, the veil is torn, and the temple is now the assembled people. The reverence Exodus commands is not less than the sacred-places version but more — it follows God's presence wherever it goes, which is now to a congregation of ordinary people in an ordinary room.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew na'al (a sandal, shoe) and chalats (to draw off, the verb of the shoe-loosing rite); Greek hypodema (that which is bound under the foot) and sandalion (a sandal).

expand to see more

Hebrew na'al (H5275) — a sandal or shoe; the word in Exodus 3:5, Ruth 4:7, and Deuteronomy 25:9.

Hebrew chalats (H2502) — to draw off, withdraw; the verb of the shoe-loosing rite, giving the name chalitzah to the ceremony.

Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem as a kinsman; the legal act the shoe-transfer confirms in Ruth 4.

Greek hypodema (G5266) — a sandal, that which is bound underneath; the word in Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16.

Greek hypodeo (G5265) — to bind under, shoe; the verb in Ephesians 6:15 rendered shod.

Usage

"“Put off thy shoes… the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” — a bush in a desert, holy because God is there."

"“A man plucked off his shoe… this was a testimony in Israel” — the legal machinery by which Boaz becomes redeemer."

"“Whose shoes I am not worthy to bear” — the lowest slave's office, chosen to measure a distance."
